item.title: Three weeks in Europe, part two: Seville to Prague
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
By Sunday, September 27th, I had been in Seville for a few days and people were arriving for the annual Discourse meetup. I honestly cannot remember doing much that day besides chilling and waiting for everyone to show up. We hung out in the common room for happy hour, then had a buffet dinner at the hotel.

After a week of mostly figuring out my own days, it was time for a schedule.

A cathedral and a questionable ceiling

Monday was officially day one of the meetup. My first group activity was a walking tour of the cathedral, followed by a tapas lunch. There were about fifteen of us.

Water was dripping from the ceiling during lunch, and we joked that it was coming from the WC. I do not know where it was actually coming from, which is probably fine.

Then it was back for happy hour and our team intro dinner. I still cannot remember the name of the restaurant.

Workshops and bowling

Tuesday was the first conference day. I went to the Future of the Internet and AI Roundtable workshops, then went bowling with my immediate infra teammates before dinner at Casa Cuna.

Somewhere in there I also bought a Pokémon manga in Spanish. My souvenirs were now ceramic tiles and Pokémon.

273 seconds

Wednesday started with lightning talks. I went first with a presentation on NixOS, then returned for "273," my take on John Cage's 4'33".

I made a slide deck with three movements that advanced automatically. Then I did not say a word for 273 seconds.

Afterward, I went to a session about term-llm. By then I needed a break, so I missed the final round of sessions. There had been a lot of people and a lot going on, and I needed some time to myself.

Another meetup tattoo

Wednesday night I continued a tradition I started at last year's meetup: getting a tattoo.

I went to Lucero Tattoo and got a birdman from Javi Juelle. He had just drawn the flash, so it is a 1/1. A little more permanent than the tiles, and much easier to get home without breaking.

Three people at the Alcázar

Thursday was the second activity day, and this time I went to the Alcázar. Our group was only three people, which was nice. It was much less hectic than trying to keep up with a group of fifteen.

We spent about three hours walking around, learning about the architecture and who ruled it when. Tickets were sold out for the two weeks after our tour, so we got very lucky.

There was also a robot lawn mower working away in the gardens. All that architecture and history, and of course I stopped to photograph the little robot doing the groundskeeping.

Our little group walked back to the hotel afterward. I mostly chilled until happy hour and the final team dinner.

Apparently I ride in carriages now

We took carriages all the way to Ozama restaurant. It is probably the most touristy thing I have ever done.

I had spent part of the previous week complaining about the carriages making Plaza de España smell like horse shit. Now I was in one.

Dinner was pretty good. There was a flamenco performance, so it was loud at first, but we were right on the Guadalquivir. The thing I remember best from the meal is the chocolate molten lava cake. That was very good.

Laundry and more cake

Friday was the final official day, but nothing was planned. After a busy couple of weeks, I needed some chill time.

I also finally needed to do laundry. I went to a laundromat near the hotel that morning, then spent most of the day taking it easy and strolling around the hotel.

Before dinner, I went back to Cafetería Tartería Chanticream for a slice of lotus cheesecake and another espresso. I had dinner at the hotel again, this time a steak. It was very good.

The little things

Not all of my photos were of landmarks. Somewhere along the way, I found a utility cover with a Supercable gecko that looked suspiciously like the SUSE mascot. Apparently even on vacation I am looking at infrastructure and thinking about Linux.

There were more tiles, too. That part of the trip clearly was not over.

And a couple of bits of graffiti worth keeping: a duck, obviously, and an apple offering juice. A fairly good summary of what catches my attention when I am walking around.

One more breakfast

Saturday was my last day in Seville. I had packed most of my things the night before, so getting ready that morning was quick. I went for one final breakfast buffet, then hung out in the common room until my 1:15 train back to Madrid.

I stayed at Only YOU Atocha, near the train station. After the Seville hotel, it was definitely a step down. The room did not feel as spacious, and it was much louder.

I did not go out that evening. I did not even eat dinner because I was planning on another Only YOU breakfast buffet the next morning.

Unfortunately, that was not as good as the Seville one either.

Back to Prague

On Sunday morning, I took the airport express bus to the airport. I had bought Fast Track security access, and getting through security was a breeze.

My flight was at 1:15 and took just under three hours. When I arrived in Prague, I took the airport Uber straight to Mama Shelter.

It felt great. Honestly, it felt like home.

After two weeks of new places, I liked knowing what I was getting into. I was comfortable there. I did not need to figure out another hotel or make a plan for the evening.

I had a burger in the hotel restaurant and chilled for the rest of the night. That was exactly what I wanted.

item.title: Three weeks in Europe, part one: Madrid to Seville
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Last year, my first trip to Europe was one week in Prague. This year I decided to make a little more of it. I am spending three weeks in Europe, starting in Madrid before heading to Seville for the annual Discourse company meetup.

I have been away from home for one week now. This is part one.

Portland to Madrid

I left Portland on September 20th and flew to Madrid through Dallas. I had only slept a few hours the night before because I thought being exhausted would help me sleep on the plane. That did not work nearly as well as I hoped.

We were already an hour late when we landed in Madrid, then it took another two hours to get off the plane and through customs. I had planned to take the train from the airport, but by then I was mostly trying to get to the hotel.

I did manage to get a Madrid Metro card. I learned later that I could have just tapped to pay.

I stayed at Hotel Artrip for three nights. The first day I got there, honestly, I slept through most of it.

Madrid might be the city that never sleeps

On my second day, I went to the center around Puerta del Sol and checked out the official Metro de Madrid store. It is a whole store for Madrid transit merchandise, which is exactly the sort of thing I will seek out while visiting a new city.

Madrid is a unique city. It might be the real city that never sleeps. It was busier at 3:30 in the morning outside my hotel than it was at 10 in the morning. I am not sure I could ever get used to the flow there.

For a person who likes documenting trips, I took exactly two pictures in Madrid. This was one of them:

On my last night, I met up with a coworker for pizza and gelato around Gran Vía, then took the Metro back to the hotel. I could not sleep and stayed up far too late even though I had a 9 a.m. train the next morning.

A much better way to travel

The other picture I took was at Madrid-Puerta de Atocha while waiting for the train to Seville.

The trip was scheduled for two hours and fifty minutes, but we arrived about ten minutes early. No one bought the seat next to me, which was a nice surprise. It was comfortable, easy, and made me wish the U.S. had a better rail system.

The long way to Triana

I went straight to Only YOU Hotel Sevilla and took a little siesta. After I got up, I walked around a bit and got a smoothie from Oakberry. Then I decided to walk around a little more to find coffee.

That turned into an hour-long walk to Muy Río, where I learned they had run out of filter coffee 45 minutes before closing. I gave up on coffee, but the walk ended up taking me right past Casa de Pilatos. I did not go inside because I was still on a coffee mission that had not officially failed yet.

Afterward, I crossed the Puente de Triana and walked around Triana looking at ceramics. Centro Cerámica Triana was closing soon, so I did not waste my money trying to rush through it. I hoped I would have time to come back.

I ate dinner at the hotel that night, and it was one of the top five meals of my life. I still need to get the names of the dishes. Somehow I found enough energy to go back out one more time for ice cream at Sibaris.

Transit cards and cake

I stayed up way too late again, slept until noon, and missed the hotel breakfast buffet.

My first task for the meetup was to get transit cards for the team. I rode the bus to Prado de San Sebastián and went to PAC Prado. After working through a little communication barrier, we did it. I left with the cards and decided to walk back to the hotel.

Later, I went to Cafetería Tartería Chanticream for queso con fresa and Muerte por Chocolate cakes with an espresso, then walked to the Setas de Sevilla. I got there around sunset and stayed long enough to watch the whole structure change as its lights came on.

On the walk home I took a picture of a random European street at night. That was apparently the theme of my photography for the day: giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, giant wooden landmark, street.

Back to Triana

The next day I took the tram instead of walking or taking the bus. I finally got a decent filter coffee at Jester Coffee, then went back to Triana. This time I made it to Centro Cerámica Triana with enough time to visit the museum. I also bought a couple of tiles, because carrying fragile ceramics around Europe for another two weeks seemed like a good idea.

A lot of what caught my attention inside was ceramic being used as graphic design: advertisements, lettering, and public signs made out of tile.

Plaza de España

The next day I walked from the hotel to NYC Icy and got lotus and chocolate ice cream, then kept going to Plaza de España. It is a pretty sweet building and plaza. The whole place is full of ceramic and stone details that are easy to miss while looking at the scale of it.

The stonework was just as good. Someone cut a bow-tie-shaped joint directly into this railing, and I probably spent longer looking at it than any normal person would.

The downside was that all the carriage rides made the plaza smell like horse shit, especially with the temperature in the high 30s C.

That makes one week away from home. I have made it to Seville, figured out the transit, found the coffee, and bought breakable souvenirs far too early in the trip. The meetup is next.

Gracias por leer.
